e-5576.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
e-5576.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ onto the plane $\mathbf{r}=s\mathbf{v}+t\mathbf{w},$ where $s,t\in\mathbb R,$ and
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069030/assets/df90590ac6801e6f2efaada175e5d8460a45cb06375064eb53f80eddbbd3991c.png)
e-5576.worked_solution:
First, notice that $\mathbf v$ and $\mathbf w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A\left(A^T\!A\right)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}\{\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{w}\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^3.$ In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069030/assets/a1592d17b242a66e66948692dfaf7892f9df6d415ae96fb59154455ffe1a4ef9.png)
Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}12 & 4 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{32}[\begin{aligned}3 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}12 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 & -2 \\ -2 & -2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}7 \\ -9\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

e-5575.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
e-5575.problem:
Verify whether the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ where
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069030/assets/226d83de1fff110426877af083e1aee5eac7f7de1244bb59f7f801aeea8ec6a5.png)
e-5575.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether $\mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}4 & 1 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 4\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}↔{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 3 & 1 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+(-3){R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-4){R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & -3 & -15\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+(-\frac{3}{2}){R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 4 \\ 0 & -2 & -10 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{x}$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
\textrm{proj}_{S} \: \mathbf{x} = A(A^T\!A)^{-1}\!A^T\,\mathbf{x}.
$$

In our case, we have
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14069030/assets/c051729499bde9389ad7e38ab91d3609c8153cbed59233f4b3e3e7ac9e9c2534.png)

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 & 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}5 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}26 & 8 \\ 8 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{14}[\begin{aligned}3 & -8 \\ -8 & 26\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 1
after.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 14\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[130211]⟹AT=[101321].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[130211]⋅([101321]⋅[130211])−1⋅[101321]⋅[3−63]=[130211]⋅[24414]−1⋅[60]=[130211]⋅16[7−2−21]⋅[60]=[130211]⋅[7−2]=[1−45]

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms p=7v−2w=(1,−4,5), option e. Independently, x−p=(2,−2,−2) has zero dot product with both v and w, proving orthogonality. The displayed incorrect submission selected d, not e.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
content.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -6 \\ 3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 14\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}7 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}7 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -4 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[2−31],w=[2−11],x=[−3−31].

a
[−2−3−1]
b
[12−3]
c
[−3−21]
d
[1−33]
e
[2−13]
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector p=2v−3w=(−2,−3,−1) lies in the plane. The residual x−p=(−1,0,2) satisfies (x−p)·v=−2+2=0 and (x−p)·w=−2+2=0. Therefore p is the orthogonal projection, option a.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane  $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ 8 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Find the orthogonal projection of x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[2−31],w=[2−11],x=[−3−31].

a
[−2−3−1]
b
[12−3]
c
[−3−21]
d
[1−33]
e
[2−13]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have

A=[||vw||]=[22−3−111]⟹AT=[2−312−11].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[22−3−111]⋅([2−312−11]⋅[22−3−111])−1⋅[2−312−11]⋅[−3−31]=[22−3−111]⋅[14886]−1⋅[4−2]=[22−3−111]⋅110[3−4−47]⋅[4−2]=[22−3−111]⋅[2−3]=[−2−3−1]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
content.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane  $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 2 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}14 & 8 \\ 8 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{10}[\begin{aligned}3 & -4 \\ -4 & 7\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ -3 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ -3 \\ -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[2−12],w=[111],x=[2−3−2].

b

decision.explanation: The vector p=v−2w=(0,−3,0) lies in the plane. The residual x−p=(2,0,−2) has dot products 4−4=0 with v and 2−2=0 with w. Thus p is the orthogonal projection, option a.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Find the orthogonal projection of the vector x onto the plane r=sv+tw, where s,t∈R, and v=[2−12],w=[111],x=[2−3−2].

a
[0−30]
b
[1−11]
c
[3−31]
d
[2−32]
e
[212]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace S spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[21−1121]⟹AT=[2−12111].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[21−1121]⋅([2−12111]⋅[21−1121])−1⋅[2−12111]⋅[2−3−2]=[21−1121]⋅[9333]−1⋅[3−3]=[21−1121]⋅16[1−1−13]⋅[3−3]=[21−1121]⋅[1−2]=[0−30]

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms p=v−2w=(0,−3,0). This lies in the plane, and x−p=(2,0,−2) is orthogonal to both v and w. Hence option a is correct. The displayed incorrect submission selected c.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
content.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -1 & 2 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -1 & 1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ -3 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The plane consists of vectors whose first and third coordinates are equal. Projecting x=(2,1,4) onto it averages those coordinates, giving p=(3,1,3). Indeed, p=(4/3)v+(1/3)w, and x−p=(−1,0,1) is orthogonal to both v and w.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the plane  $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace $S$ spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

 

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1 \\ 4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 3 \\ 3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}13 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}1 & -1 \\ -1 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}13 \\ 5\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{6}[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 1 & -1 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 \\ 9 & 14\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 23\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{45}[\begin{aligned}14 & -9 \\ -9 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 23\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

First, notice that v and w are linearly independent.

The orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix A is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace S=Span{v,w} in R3. In our case, we have A=[||vw||]=[132221]⟹AT=[122321].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[132221]⋅([122321]⋅[132221])−1⋅[122321]⋅[29−1]=[132221]⋅[99914]−1⋅[1823]=[132221]⋅145[14−9−99]⋅[1823]=[132221]⋅[11]=[443]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Plane
content.problem:
Find the orthogonal projection of the vector $x$ onto the plane $r=sv+tw,$ where $s,t\in R,$ and

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2 \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,w=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9 \\ -1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that $v$ and $w$ are linearly independent. 

The orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

Since our plane passes through the origin, it defines the subspace $S=\text{Span}{v,w}$ in ${R}^{3}.$ In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ v & w \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 & 2 \\ 3 & 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ 9 \\ -1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}9 & 9 \\ 9 & 14\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 23\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{45}[\begin{aligned}14 & -9 \\ -9 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ 23\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 3 \\ 2 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}4 \\ 4 \\ 3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The closest vector is the orthogonal projection. The vector p=(1/6)a₁+(1/2)a₂=(0,1,0) belongs to the subspace. Its residual x−p=(1,0,1) has zero dot product with both a₁ and a₂, proving that p is the closest vector.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[−333],a2=[11−1],x=[111].

EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[−31313−1]⇒AT=[−33311−1].

Therefore, we get the following projection:

projSx=[−31313−1]⋅([−33311−1]⋅[−31313−1])−1⋅[−33311−1]⋅[111]=[−31313−1]⋅[27−3−33]−1⋅[31]=[−31313−1]⋅124[1119]⋅[31]=[−31313−1]⋅[1612]=[010]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
content.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-3 \\ 3 \\ 3\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}-3 & 3 & 3 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}27 & -3 \\ -3 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{24}[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 9\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-3 & 1 \\ 3 & 1 \\ 3 & -1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{6} \\ \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

a
[12−1]
b
[3−2−1]
c
[−31−3]
d
[32−3]
e
[1−2−3]
Submit

decision.explanation: The vector p=a₁−2a₂=(1,−2,−3) lies in the subspace. The residual x−p=(1,−4,3) satisfies (x−p)·a₁=3−3=0 and (x−p)·a₂=1−4+3=0. Thus p is the orthogonal projection and the unique closest vector.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where a1=[30−1],a2=[111],x=[2−60].

a
[12−1]
b
[3−2−1]
c
[−31−3]
d
[32−3]
e
[1−2−3]
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[3101−11]⟹AT=[30−1111].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[3101−11]⋅([30−1111]⋅[3101−11])−1⋅[30−1111]⋅[2−60]=[3101−11]⋅[10223]−1⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅126[3−2−210]⋅[6−4]=[3101−11]⋅[1−2]=[1−2−3]

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms p=a₁−2a₂=(1,−2,−3), option e. Independently, x−p=(1,−4,3) has zero dot product with both spanning vectors, so p is the unique closest vector. The displayed incorrect submission selected d.

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
content.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 0 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 & 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -6 \\ 0\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}10 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{26}[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 10\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}6 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The vector p=10a₁−4a₂=(2,2,8) belongs to the subspace. The residual x−p=(6,−6,0) has zero dot product with both a₁ and a₂. Therefore p is the orthogonal projection and the unique closest vector, option c.

after.name: Question 8
after.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where 

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 0\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ -4 \\ 8\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ -4 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 0 \\ 2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ -4 \\ 8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}2 & 4 \\ 4 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}6 & -2 \\ -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}4 \\ -8\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 0 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ -4\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 2 \\ 8\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 9
after.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}14 & 9 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -9 \\ -9 & 14\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
content.problem:
Verify whether the vectors ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent, and find the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the vectors ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}},$ where

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, we verify whether ${a}_{1},{a}_{2},{a}_{3}$ are linearly independent. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

$$
\begin{aligned} & [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 & 0 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & -1\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{1}↔{R}_{3}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ -3 & -2 & 1 \\ 2 & 1 & 0\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{2}:={R}_{2}+3{R}_{1} \\ {R}_{3}:={R}_{3}-2{R}_{1}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & -1 & 2\end{aligned}] &  & \begin{aligned}{R}_{3}:={R}_{3}+{R}_{2}\end{aligned} \\  & ∼[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & -1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 \\ 0 & 0 & 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

In the reduced matrix above, the pivot columns correspond to the linearly independent vectors ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ that form the basis of our span.

Now, the orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace spanned by the linearly independent columns of a matrix $A$ is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\,⇒\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 & -3 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}3 \\ -1 \\ 1\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}14 & 9 \\ 9 & 6\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{3}[\begin{aligned}6 & -9 \\ -9 & 14\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}10 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ -3 & -2 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The vector p=(11/2)a₁−(3/4)a₂=(7,4,7) lies in the subspace. The residual x−p=(1,0,−1) is orthogonal to both a₁ and a₂. Thus p is the orthogonal projection and the unique closest vector, option b.

after.name: Question 10
after.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where   

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{32}[\begin{aligned}12 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}22 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Find the vector in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} that is closest to the vector x, where

a1=[111],a2=[−22−2],x=[846].

EXPLANATION

First, notice that a1 and a2 are linearly independent.

The closest vector to x in the subspace spanned by {a1,a2} is orthogonal projection of x onto the subspace, which is given by projSx=A(ATA)−1ATx.

In our case, we have A=[||a1a2||]=[1−2121−2]⟹AT=[111−22−2].

Therefore, we get the following projection: projSx=[1−2121−2]⋅([111−22−2]⋅[1−2121−2])−1⋅[111−22−2]⋅[846]=[1−2121−2]⋅[3−2−212]−1⋅[18−20]=[1−2121−2]⋅132[12223]⋅[18−20]=14[1−2121−2]⋅[22−3]=[747]

content.knowledge_point: Finding the Orthogonal Projection of a Vector Onto a Subspace
content.problem:
Find the vector in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ 
that is closest to the vector $x,$ where   

$$
{a}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}],\,{a}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 2 \\ -2\end{aligned}],\,x=[\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}].
$$
content.worked_solution:
First, notice that ${a}_{1}$ and ${a}_{2}$ are linearly independent. 

The closest vector to $x$ in the subspace spanned by ${{a}_{1},{a}_{2}}$ is orthogonal projection of $x$ onto the subspace, which is given by

$$
{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x=A({A}^{T}\,A)^{-1}\,{A}^{T}\,x.
$$

In our case, we have

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ {a}_{1} & {a}_{2} \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\,⟹\,{A}^{T}=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we get the following projection:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\text{proj}}_{S}\,x & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {([\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}])}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 & 1 & 1 \\ -2 & 2 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}8 \\ 4 \\ 6\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot {[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ -2 & 12\end{aligned}]}^{-1}\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot \frac{1}{32}[\begin{aligned}12 & 2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}18 \\ -20\end{aligned}] \\  & =\frac{1}{4}[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ 1 & 2 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}22 \\ -3\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}7 \\ 4 \\ 7\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$
